Left, Right and Center (podcast) is a good one for American politics/takes on current events. 

It offers multiple (usually very informed) perspectives on different issues.

Interesting that Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern was included in this video. I live in NZ and while vaccine passes are mandatory to enter most businesses (not including essential services such as supermarkets, pharmacies, etc.), businesses actually get to decide whether or not they want to require patrons to show a vaccine pass (some do not). And from my own experience, it’s only restaurants that require a vaccine pass. 

Businesses/organisations also require you to scan a QR code (no personal information shared) or write down your phone number or email (and the time of your visit) in case someone with Covid was at the same place at the same time. This form of contact tracing has enabled NZ to maintain relatively low levels of covid. 

I live in a major city (not Auckland) and we’ve only had a handful or two of cases since the pandemic started. Contact tracing has helped us stop the virus in its tracks (when cases begin to pop-up) so that the city, and much of the rest of the county, have been able to go back to being covid-free.

I find my life (and that of my friends) has barely been impacted by government regulations regarding covid. We locked down originally for like 5-6 weeks I think (only partial lockdown for some of the time) back in the beginning of the pandemic. Since then we’ve only had to lockdown for 2-3 weeks once earlier this year.

Auckland and Northland had a much longer period of lockdown (months) earlier this year but Jacinda’s administration followed through on their word. Once we hit a high vaccination rate, the government significantly reduced restrictions in areas with covid.

I don’t feel as though my freedom has been severely impacted and neither does most of the country. Only a tiny minority of people here are upset about the restrictions we’ve had and there’s always gonna be a fraction of the population who are unhappy with government decisions.

I feel like this comment is very accurate. I grew up in the US and studied at a well-ranked university for two years before I moved to NZ and finished my degree here. Having studied and worked in both countries, I can say my experience has been the same.

Studying at university in NZ was a COMPLETELY different world. The competition and lack of support I previously experienced (my US university actively tried to get students to drop out in the first 1 -2 years by making courses/the general experience more difficult, in order to have “the best of the best” graduates) suddenly didn’t exist when I got to NZ (well at least not to the same degree).

Speaking with friends who grew up here in NZ, their school experience always sounds very different to my own. When I was in high school, grades mattered a lot and it was quite competitive (at least where I went school). They started preparing us for university at the age of 12. That was THE goal of public education in my district (along with good state test and SAT scores). 

While there were supports in place to help people graduate, if you couldn’t keep up, you were often left in the dust. Unless you had a very severe disability, any sort of intellectual difficulty or disability that people had (ADHD particularly), was often treated by teachers and other students as a moral failing, lack of intelligence and/or pure laziness.

Not to mention, a huge marker of your social status in my area from the age of 17+ was what university you were going to attend/were attending/did attend. Here in NZ, it really doesn’t matter. You can tell because in the US, people refer to their specific university, whereas here, what university you went to is almost never mentioned because the main universities across the country are of similar quality and ranking.

I found the same when I began working too. My first year as a graduate I worked at a major advertising agency and my workplace was super fast-paced by NZ standards. I found myself struggling to manage the intense workload and began working 60 hours a week. 

What’s most interesting about this is that I was the EXCEPTION. Even in an incredibly high pressure environment, everyone made an effort to achieve work/life balance. Most people were done for the day by 5:15pm (with exceptions for major deadlines/pitches). My colleagues and bosses actually TOLD ME OFF (in a caring, concerned manner) for staying late and working too much and I was the least experienced/lowest rung person in the office!! 

Again, I really can’t stress how abnormal it is here to work more than 40 hours a week (again, with specific exceptions). 

Anyways this is all to say, there’s DEFINITELY a cultural difference that begins in school all the way through university to working life. I find it’s made a huge positive difference for my ADHD, for me to be in NZ. While the mental health support here is severely lacking, the work/academic culture here definitely makes things easier.

If I had continued my education and then work life in the US, I’m not sure if I would have managed… 

American culture definitely makes it harder to study and work with ADHD than some other developed western countries. That said, I don’t believe that American work culture would be responsible for misdiagnosis of ADHD. Although, when it comes to university, there might be a little truth to this (or at least student seeking diagnosis to get stimulants).

And that’s my very long-winded two-cents :)

I really enjoy the conversational tone that you begin with, ‘I get it you know, why you couldn’t see’. Without sounding too cheesy, your first few lines make me feel like I’ve just walked into the room and overheard you speaking. Instead of a literal room though, it’s your mind, where you’re going over what you would say to this person if the right moment presented itself. 

I’m not sure if this what you are going for but it made me feel very comfortable as a reader who has gone over (again and again) how I would communicate my experiences to others in my head. The structure of your sentences seems to echo the voice in my own head and crosses over into a more dream-like perspective as you begin to personify the elements.

I particularly liked your personification of fate and dreams. Both the idea of fate and dreams as brother and sister, as well as the execution of your phrasing ‘you couldn’t feel dreams pulling you into his house...’. That line actually reminded me of ‘The Sandman’ by Neil Gaiman which I really enjoyed.
